 She Paid a Hospital Bill Out of Pocket in 2018 and Kept the Receipt. At 70 Her HSA Can Still Pay Her Back, Tax-Free
 By David Beren 
 Published November 18, 2026, 8:29am ET · 4 min read 
 Life After Work desk. Editor: David Beren .
 𝕏 
 f 
 ⧉ 
 Quick Read
 The IRS sets no deadline for HSA reimbursements, so old medical bills paid out of pocket can still become tax-free cash years later.
 Reimbursement only works if the HSA existed before the expense, insurance never paid it, and you never itemized it as a deduction.
 Medicare enrollment stops HSA contributions but leaves qualified withdrawals tax-free, though weak records trigger income tax on the money.

 One important thing to know is that  Health Savings Account (HSA) holders can reimburse themselves tax-free for qualified medical expenses paid years earlier. If someone has had a health savings account since before a 2018 hospital bill, they can still claim that bill tax-free. The IRS sets no deadline for reimbursing yourself from an HSA for old medical expenses.
 This means a 70-year-old can reimburse herself now for a bill she paid out of pocket years ago, as long as the expense qualifies and the paperwork supports it. The reimbursement covers money she already spent on qualified care.
 How an Old Hospital Bill Becomes a Tax-Free Withdrawal
 An HSA can reimburse you for a qualified medical expense at any time after you pay it, whether that’s the same week or many years later, as long as three conditions apply. The first is that the expense has to have been incurred after the HSA was established. Second, insurance or anyone else can’t have already reimbursed it. Lastly, it can’t have been claimed as an itemized deduction. If all three hold true, the withdrawal is free of federal income tax, and the cash can go into a checking account to spend on anything .
 Where the IRS Puts It in Writing
 Under 26 U.S.C. § 223(f)(1) [ 1 ] , any amount paid or distributed from an HSA “which is used exclusively to pay qualified medical expenses of any account beneficiary shall not be includible in gross income.” [ 1 ] The statute doesn’t say when that reimbursement has to happen.
 IRS Publication 969 adds that “you don’t have to make withdrawals from your HSA each year.” The publication also spells out the records to keep: proof that the distributions were exclusively to pay or reimburse qualified medical expenses, hadn’t been previously paid or reimbursed from another source, and hadn’t been taken as an itemized deduction in any year.
 Who Qualifies for a Late Reimbursement and Who Doesn’t
 Everything depends on the date the account opened. Publication 969 states that expenses incurred before you establish your HSA aren’t qualified medical expenses, and that state law determines when an HSA is established. If her account opened after that hospital stay, the receipt has no HSA value. Qualified expenses also cover you, your spouse, and dependents you claim on your return.
 Medicare Stops Contributions but Leaves Spending Open
 Medicare affects only the money going in. Under 26 U.S.C. § 223(b)(7) [ 1 ] , the contribution limit drops to zero starting with the first month a person is entitled to Medicare. Withdrawals for qualified expenses keep working. Publication 969 says that if you are no longer eligible, you can still receive tax-free distributions to pay or reimburse qualified medical expenses.
 Steps to Pay Yourself Back From an HSA
 Get the date your HSA was established from the trustee, and confirm it is before the bill date.
 Pull together the itemized bill, proof of payment, and the insurer’s explanation of benefits showing the amount insurance didn’t cover.
 Ask the HSA trustee for a distribution equal to the unreimbursed amount. The trustee reports it on Form 1099-SA.
 Report the distribution on Form 8889 and file it with your tax return. A distribution used for qualified medical expenses isn’t taxed, but you still have to report it.
 File the receipts with your tax records. Publication 969 says, “Don’t send these records with your tax return.”
 Some savers set this up on purpose. They pay medical bills from regular cash while they’re working, leave the HSA invested to grow, and save the receipts for withdrawals later. For 2026, people still eligible to contribute can put in up to $4,400 with self-only coverage and $8,750 with family coverage.
 Once you’re 65 or older, Medicare premiums also count as qualified expenses, though Medigap premiums don’t. So the 2026 Part B premium of $202.90 [ 2 ] a month can be paid from the account, too. Part B is only the headline cost, though; IRMAA surcharges and coverage gaps catch many retirees off guard, which is why we mapped out the full set of Medicare surprises in a free guide here .
 Mistakes That Can Make an Old Receipt Taxable
 Missing paperwork is one risk. If your records can’t show the expense qualified, the withdrawal is taxed as income under § 223(f)(2) [ 1 ] , and Publication 969 notes an additional 20% tax can apply on top. Under § 223(f)(4)(C) [ 1 ] , that extra tax goes away once the account holder reaches Medicare eligibility age, but regular income tax still applies.
 Claiming the same expense twice is another way to lose the tax break. Publication 969 says you can’t deduct qualified medical expenses as an itemized deduction on Schedule A that equal a tax-free HSA distribution. A bill you already deducted on an old return can’t be reimbursed tax-free now. Contributions have a separate Medicare rule. If your enrollment is backdated, any HSA contributions made during the retroactive coverage period are considered excess.
 For account holders with old medical receipts and an HSA that was open when those bills were paid, each documented, unreimbursed, and never-deducted receipt can still be reimbursed tax-free.
